auxiliary_material: The study noted that less physically active participants were more likely to experience a significant increase in Lachnospiraceae, indicating host lifestyle factors may modify the microbiome response to dietary intervention. The efficacy validation relied on syngeneic mouse models (C57BL/6) receiving human fecal microbiota transplantation, rather than direct clinical outcome measurement in the human participants. The abstract does not specify whether the human participants were concurrently receiving ICI therapy or if their clinical tumor response was measured.
outline_action: Cite this study as evidence that human dietary interventions can modulate specific taxa (Lachnospiraceae) capable of enhancing ICI response in preclinical models. Explicitly distinguish this from a clinical efficacy trial, noting that the human ICI outcome link is inferred via fecal transplant rather than direct patient response data. Continue searching for interventional trials where human participants receive both the dietary modification and ICI therapy with reported clinical endpoints.
remaining_gap: The success criterion requires evidence of improved ICI efficacy within the human cohort receiving the dietary intervention. This study demonstrates the causal chain only up to the point of human microbiome modulation, with efficacy outcomes measured exclusively in mouse models receiving human stool. It remains unconfirmed whether the observed microbiome changes directly translate to improved survival or tumor response in humans undergoing ICI treatment.
useful_material: This study conducted a randomized, cross-over dietary intervention trial (BEWELL Study, NCT04267874) in which participants consumed black raspberry (BRB) nectar versus placebo. The authors reported a significant increase in the abundance of Lachnospiraceae in human stool following the BRB intervention. To assess the impact on immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) efficacy, participant stool samples (pre- and post-intervention) were transferred into tumor-bearing mouse models (MC38, CMT167) treated with anti-PD1. The study found that stool collected after the dietary intervention was associated with smaller tumor volumes in mice compared to pre-intervention stool, and specific Lachnospiraceae isolates supplemented into pre-intervention stool recapitulated this tumor suppression. This provides a human-derived dietary intervention linked to microbiome changes that functionally enhance ICI response in a preclinical model.
